an2.21:2.1: _Paṇḍita_ is normally used for a learned scholar, rather than a contemplative “sage”. Pali has many more terms for “a wise person” than does English, and it is not easy to distinguish the senses. “Astute” is meant to convey the sense of one who is observant and of sound judgment. In early Sanskrit it is a desirable quality of a daughter or son (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.17–18), and is a synonym of _medhāvī_ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2) and _dhīra_ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.5), but less exalted than _muni_ or brahmin (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1).
an2.21:2.3: When a monastic realizes they have transgressed, they should seek out another monastic and confess, naming the action and the type of offense. Any monastic will do, as seniority is not a consideration here. Unless the confessing monastic is mistaken—for example if they think they transgressed but in fact did not—the receiving monastic acknowledges the fact that the offense was committed, and ensures that the confessing monastic understands the nature of the offense. Then they urge the confessing monastic to restrain themselves in the future. This process is seen in the Suttas (eg. [an3.91:3.13]() and formalized in the Vinaya ([pli-tv-kd2:27.1.8]()). In most cases this is sufficient to clear the offense, but in some cases a material object must be relinquished, while more serious offenses require suspension or even expulsion.
an2.22:1.1: This introduces a series of passages on scriptural fidelity. Throughout the Suttas, the Buddha has amiable conversations with people who disagree with him, but is stern with those who misrepresent his teachings. He intended his teachings to be clear, and he expected his students to represent these accurately.
an2.22:1.3: “Wrongly grasped” like the man who grasps a snake by the tail ([mn22:10.10]()).
an2.23:1.3: For the first case, see [an3.57](), for the second, see [sn42.13]().
an2.23:2.3: Not everything in the Suttas is spoken by the Buddha. This includes, obviously, statements by other people in the Suttas, as well as the settings and narrative backgrounds, which were added by redactors. For the bulk of the shorter Suttas, where setting and attribution are absent, it is conventionally assumed that the Buddha is speaking. This may be so, but the traditions did not always agree on such attributions, so it is wise to exercise caution.
an2.24:1.3: “In need of interpretation” is _neyyattha_, literally, “whose meaning is to be drawn out”, while _nītattha_ is one whose “meaning has been drawn out”, i.e. “explicit”. The exact sense of these is not defined in the early texts, and in later debates, Buddhist schools have the uncanny habit of concluding that *their* favorite teachings are explicit, while those that disagree with them require interpretation. We should rather seek to understand this distinction in terms of the Suttas themselves. On multiple occasions, students seek someone to explain the meaning in detail of a brief statement ([mn18:10.7]()), a distinction which we already met in the previous chapter ([an2.14:1.1]()). Some verses are obviously meant as riddles or paradoxes, such as [dhp294]() which advocates killing parents. More generally, the Suttas routinely present teachings through the use of technical terms whose meaning is explained elsewhere, for example the _vibhaṅga_ Suttas such as [sn12.2]() or [sn45.8]().
an2.26:1.1: This often describes a false mendicant who is “underhand”, literally “hides their deeds” ([an3.13:4.5]()).
an2.27:1.1: This is a good example of a text requiring interpretation. This statement cannot be taken as absolute, as some wrong views are compatible with a heavenly rebirth; even Divinities hold the view of eternalism ([sn6.4]()). Where this statement is found with more context, the wrong view is part of a wider pattern of bad behavior ([dn12:9.4](), [mn57](), [sn42.3]()).
